name: Social Determinants of Health
title: Social Determinants of Health
answer: Social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age, including income, education, housing, food security, employment, neighborhood safety, and social support. In epidemiology and population health, they are studied as upstream causes of disease, injury, and health inequity, not as clinical diagnoses. AI enters this field when models use social and economic data to predict health risks, stratify populations, or guide the allocation of services. The scope also covers the measurement of structural factors such as racism, segregation, and access to care, which shape individual exposures.

sections.body: Social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age, including income, education, housing, food security, employment, neighborhood safety, and social support. In epidemiology and population health, they are studied as upstream causes of disease, injury, and health inequity, not as clinical diagnoses. AI enters this field when models use social and economic data to predict health risks, stratify populations, or guide the allocation of services. The scope also covers the measurement of structural factors such as racism, segregation, and access to care, which shape individual exposures.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The infrastructure includes electronic health records, administrative claims, census and survey data, and geographic information systems. Work often runs on cloud platforms with secure enclaves, because social determinant data is sensitive and often linked across sectors. Privacy-preserving record linkage and federated learning are used when data cannot be pooled. Data pipelines must handle missing values, different geographies, and irregular update cycles.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with defining the population and the outcome, then assembling social determinant variables from multiple sources. Analysts link these variables to health records, build statistical or machine learning models, and test whether predictions hold across groups. Causal methods, such as regression adjustment or propensity scores, are used when the goal is to estimate the effect of a social factor rather than just predict risk. Validation includes fairness audits, calibration checks, and review by community representatives. Deployment often means embedding risk scores into care management workflows, not making autonomous decisions.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Social determinant data carries privacy, consent, and anti-discrimination obligations, because it can reveal income, housing instability, immigration status, or race. Provenance matters: teams must document where each variable comes from, how it was collected, and whether individuals or communities agreed to its use. Risks include stigmatization, misclassification, and the reinforcement of historical inequities if models are trained on biased data. The site maintains 219 compliance and regulation pages, and social determinant work touches on many of the same privacy and data protection rules.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward routine collection of social determinant data in clinical settings, with standardized screening questions and codes. AI is being applied to predict social risk, match patients to resources, and evaluate community-level interventions. Expect more attention to community data governance, model transparency, and evidence that these tools reduce rather than widen disparities. Interoperability between health, housing, and social services systems will shape what is possible. The long-term test is whether these models improve population health outcomes, not just prediction accuracy.
